questions.q: In an active-passive multi-region pattern, which region serves live production traffic?
options: Only the primary region; the secondary is a standby that does not serve user traffic until failover
Both regions serve live traffic simultaneously
Neither region serves traffic directly — a third region always sits in front
Whichever region currently has the lowest replication lag
questions.explain: In active-passive, one region — the primary — serves all live traffic, while the secondary is a standby (cold, warm, or hot) that only begins serving traffic after a failover is declared.

questions.q: What real-world gap does this lesson say almost always exists in an active-passive design, regardless of what the documented RPO claims?
options: A permanent doubling of infrastructure cost
A requirement to rewrite the application in a different language for the secondary region
A small window of in-flight writes that existed in the primary but never reached the secondary before failure — replication lag
A mandatory 24-hour waiting period before failover is allowed
questions.explain: Because replication to the standby is rarely perfectly synchronous, there is almost always a small window of writes that made it to the primary but not the secondary before a failure — that lag is the real-world RPO.

questions.q: What new engineering problem does active-active introduce that active-passive does not have to solve?
options: The need for a DNS record, which active-passive does not use at all
Conflict resolution for records that could be written in either region at nearly the same time, since both regions serve live traffic simultaneously
The need to provision any infrastructure in the secondary region at all
A requirement to use a different cloud provider for each region
questions.explain: Because both regions in active-active accept writes, the same record can be written in two places at nearly the same time, requiring conflict resolution, multi-master replication, or deliberate write partitioning — a problem active-passive's one-directional replication never creates.

questions.q: Why does active-active typically cost more than active-passive, independent of whether a failure ever occurs?
options: Active-active requires a more expensive support contract with the cloud provider
Active-active always requires more Availability Zones per region
Active-active only works with a single specific database engine
Both regions in active-active run full production capacity continuously, rather than capacity that mostly sits idle until needed
questions.explain: Active-active means both regions are serving live traffic at full production capacity all the time, so you are paying for two complete production environments simultaneously and continuously, whether or not a failure ever happens.

questions.q: A workload has an RTO of several hours and an RPO of tens of minutes. According to this lesson's guidance on choosing a pattern, which approach best fits?
options: Active-active, because it is always the safer default regardless of the actual targets
A warm active-passive standby, which can meet both targets at a fraction of active-active's running cost
No DR pattern is needed since the RTO is more than one hour
A cold pilot-light standby is disqualified by definition and must be upgraded to active-active
questions.explain: An RTO of hours and an RPO of tens of minutes are well within what a warm active-passive standby can deliver, so paying for active-active's continuous dual-region capacity and synchronization complexity would not be justified by the actual targets.
